edge.title: The phone that is pointed, not used
edge.setup: You're in a crowded metro coach or a bus. Someone nearby holds a phone still at chest or hip height, lens toward you, thumb nowhere near the screen. You tell yourself you are imagining it, and by the time you are sure, the doors have opened and they are gone.
edge.tell: A phone held still with the lens toward you and no one touching the screen.
move: Act before the next stop: say loudly, 'Please stop recording me', so people around you hear it.
Ask a co-passenger to stay as a witness and alert metro or bus staff, so the person cannot slip away at the doors.
Note the coach, station and time, then file a police complaint the same day.
edge.why: Filming works only while it goes unnoticed and the person can leave. Naming it aloud, in front of witnesses, before the doors open removes both. Delay is the filmer's whole advantage, so the move is to act in the first minute.
edge.variants: Same shape: a lens under a changing-room gap, a phone angled up a stairwell, a 'selfie' with you deliberately in the frame.

scenario.question: You are standing in a crowded Namma Metro coach on your way home. The man next to you has held his phone still at hip height for two stops, lens pointed at you, thumb nowhere near the screen. The next station is a minute away. What do you do?

choices.text: Say loudly, 'Please stop recording me', ask the person beside you to stay as a witness, and alert metro staff at the next stop so he cannot slip out.
Wait until you are completely sure before making a scene. You might be imagining it.
Say nothing now, get off at your stop and decide later whether it is worth reporting.
Quietly move to the other end of the coach so you are out of frame.

lens.name: Concentrated benefits, diffuse costs
lens.one_line: A small charge spread across many people survives because no single person loses enough to fight it, while the one collecting it gains a lot.
lens.detail: Fifteen rupees from one customer is not worth an afternoon; fifteen rupees from every customer is real money to the shop. Each victim does the sensible sum and lets it go, so the practice continues for everyone. The cost of objecting, not the size of the wrong, decides what persists. Fixes work by lowering that cost or pooling the losses: cheap complaint forums, penalties larger than the overcharge, published rulings others can cite.
elsewhere: Convenience fees added at the last step of an online booking.
A society maintenance line item nobody can explain but nobody questions.
Bank charges of a few rupees each that add up over a year.
lens.test: Is this too small for me to fight, and is that exactly why it is being charged?
lens.today: A Bengaluru consumer forum has held Blinkit guilty of deficiency in service over a ₹479 chocolate pack in which three of six bars had expired two months earlier, The Times of India reports, and a restaurant has been fined ₹10,000 for a ₹15 carry bag. Both losses were too small for most people to pursue, which is why such practices last. Each ruling lowers the cost of the next complaint, because the next customer can cite it.

moved.what: A Bengaluru techie lost ₹5.5 lakh in fraud on AMEX and RBL credit cards without making any transactions or sharing any OTPs, The Times of India reports.
moved.so_what: Not sharing an OTP is not full protection. Turn on SMS and app alerts for every card tonight, including ones you rarely use, and report any charge you did not make to the bank in writing the same day: under RBI rules, how quickly you report decides how much of the loss you have to bear.

moved.what: EPIC numbers deleted during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls in Bengaluru have been reissued to different people, The Hindu reports, as the state turns to the city's civic polls.
moved.so_what: Search your EPIC number on the Election Commission's voter portal and check that it still shows your name and address. If it does not, raise it now, while the rolls are still being revised, not on polling day.

moved.what: Consumer commissions have ruled against Blinkit over expired chocolates in a ₹479 order, and ordered a flying academy to pay ₹10 lakh to a man whose course never started after more than two years, The Times of India reports.
moved.so_what: For quick-commerce orders, check expiry dates at the door and photograph anything wrong before you throw it away. For any course or service paid upfront, keep the receipt and written promises: the commission route works for ₹479 and for ₹10 lakh.

moved.what: The Supreme Court has rejected Karnataka's plea in the bike-taxi case, YourStory reports, meaning the services may return to Bengaluru.
moved.so_what: Do not change your commute plans yet. When services restart, book only through the app and check the plate matches; a rider offering a ride off the app is outside any insurance or complaint system.

moved.what: The Supreme Court has barred coercive action against about 4,500 homebuyers of a stalled Bengaluru project until they get possession of their flats, Deccan Herald reports.
moved.so_what: If you are paying EMIs on a stalled under-construction flat, this order is worth reading closely and showing to your lender or lawyer; keep every demand letter and payment record.

carry_over.prompt: A buyer shows you a UPI success screen with the right amount and your name, says his bank is slow, and reaches for the phone you are selling; what counts as proof you were paid?
carry_over.answer: Confirmation came from their screen, not from your bank.

quiz.question: How much did a Bengaluru techie lose in the AMEX and RBL card fraud reported this week, without sharing any OTP?
quiz.why: The Times of India: techie loses ₹5.5 lakh in AMEX, RBL card fraud with no transactions made and no OTPs shared.

quiz.question: In the Blinkit case, how many of the six chocolates in the ₹479 gift pack had expired?
quiz.why: The Times of India: 3 of 6 chocolates had expired two months earlier; the consumer forum held Blinkit guilty of deficiency in service.

quiz.question: How many homebuyers of a stalled Bengaluru project are protected by the Supreme Court's order against coercive action?
quiz.why: Deccan Herald and Verdictum: nearly 4,500 homebuyers protected until they get possession.

quiz.question: How much did the consumer commission order the flying academy to pay the man whose pilot course never started?
quiz.why: The Times of India: he paid the academy ₹10 lakh and the commission ordered ₹10 lakh to be paid to him.

quiz.question: How much funding was announced from venture capital firms at the Future Makers Conclave at the Bengaluru Tech Summit?
quiz.why: Deccan Herald: ₹1,050 crore from 24 venture capital firms.
